• A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys; weak keys were published to browser root stores
• An independent researcher found the weak keys could be reverse-engineered, possibly with AI-assisted techniques, and reported it to Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla
• Company confirms infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached, and physical and logical security controls remained intact
• Global TLS business is a very small part of operations at around 1% of company revenue, though reputational risks cannot be quantified
• Working directly with affected customers on replacement certificates; root-cause investigation ongoing with root programs

Key points:

• 990 MW (AC) solar portfolio under the PM-KUSUM scheme, spread across Maharashtra.

• 25-year PPA with MSEDCL at a fixed tariff of 3.10/unit, covering the entire generation.

• 3,900 crore estimated project cost, with project debt sanctioned, subject to financing conditions.

• Strategic optionality: Transrail may increase its stake, potentially up to 100%, subject to mutually agreed terms and approvals.

 👉This is a strategic move from executing power infrastructure projects to owning a renewable generation asset with long-term contracted offtake.

Project commissioning, financing and debt drawdown, execution timelines, and eventual returns on the investment.

IXIGO – MANAGEMENT INTERVIEW AFTER Q2FY27 RESULTS
#Q2FY27

Quarterly Performance
- Revenue grew 13% YoY to ₹321 crore.
- EBITDA stood at ₹18 crore, with 5.5% margins.
- PAT reached ₹63 crore, including ~₹40 crore stake-sale gain.
- GTV increased 22% YoY to ₹5,304 crore.

Business-Line Performance
- Flights GTV grew 37%, despite industry passenger weakness.
- Flight passenger-segment growth stood at 8%.
- Bus GTV grew 32%, alongside profitability.
- Train business performance improved sequentially.
- Revenue mix: trains 46%, flights 26%, buses 25.3%, hotels 2.5%.

Hotel Business Expansion
- Hotel GTV surged approximately 160% to ₹111 crore.
- Hotel revenue exceeded ₹8 crore, growing over 6x.
- Bookings reached approximately 4.7 lakh room nights.
- Existing users contributed 86% of hotel bookings.
- Contribution-margin profitability targeted within 2–3 years.
- Aims to become India's largest OTA by room nights in 4–5 years.
- Operating leverage elsewhere supports hotel investment.

Freshbus Investment
- ixigo reduced its Freshbus stake to approximately 8%.
- Stake sale generated around ₹40 crore in gains.
- Investment provided insights into bus-operator requirements.
- Management indicated decent returns from the investment.

Bus Business Outlook
- Only around 25% of bus bookings occur online.
- Market remains underpenetrated, offering growth opportunities.
- Bus GTV and margins have grown consistently.
- Profitability alongside growth remains a key strength.

Flight Demand & Customer Incentives
- High fares and West Asia-related headwinds affected demand.
- ixigo is incentivising train users to explore flight bookings.
- Management hopes the fare-related pressure proves temporary.

AI & Technology
- AI handles approximately 93% of chat interactions.
- Over 80% of voice calls are AI-driven end-to-end.
- AI supports customer service while controlling operating costs.
- App ratings improved to 4.8; ConfirmTkt reached 4.9.
- Investments continue in ixigo PLANX and Tara voice assistant.

Key Takeaway
- Hotels offer significant growth potential but require continued investment.
- Bus growth combines online-market expansion with profitability.
- Flight demand remains exposed to fares and external headwinds.
- AI adoption may improve service efficiency and scalability.
- Reported PAT benefited materially from the Freshbus stake-sale gain.
- Impact: Positive, with execution and profitability risks

FEDERAL BANK – MANAGEMENT INTERVIEW AFTER Q2FY27 RESULTS
#Q2FY27

Financial Performance
- Net profit rose 45% YoY to a record ₹1,386 Cr.
- Operating profit increased 35% YoY.
- Advances grew 22% YoY; deposits increased 19%.
- NII increased, while NIM improved to 3.32%.
- Cost-to-income ratio declined to 52.08%, down nearly 200 bps YoY.
- RoA stood at 1.32%; RoE remained above 13.5%.
- Management targets RoA of 1.5% within six quarters.

Credit Growth & Business Mix
- Management retained mid-teens advances growth guidance.
- High-teens growth remains possible under favourable conditions.
- Commercial banking loans grew 25% YoY.
- Commercial banking growth averaged 6–7% QoQ.
- Medium-yielding assets grew 21–22%.
- Gold loan growth remained above 35%.
- LAP grew 11%; core agriculture grew just 1% QoQ.
- Selective lending reflects risk-adjusted growth priorities.
- Focus remains on gold loans, LAP and commercial vehicles.
- MFI, credit cards and personal loans remain growth areas.

NIM & Funding Outlook
- NIM improved from 3% to 3.32%.
- Management expects quarterly NIM improvement of 4–6 bps.
- Guidance remains around 5–6 bps per quarter for upcoming quarters.
- Improvement may not be linear.
- Repo-linked assets account for approximately 45–46% of the book.
- Faster asset repricing should benefit margins after repo hikes.
- Deposit repricing may take 15–18 months.
- FCNR(B) funding and higher deposit rates create margin pressure.
- FCNR(B) impact on Q2 NIM was approximately 1 bp QoQ.
- Cost of funds declined 3 bps to 5.18%.
- FCNR(B) mobilisation reached approximately ₹14,500–15,000 Cr.
- Funds are being used to retire high-cost deposits.

Asset Quality & Credit Costs
- Gross NPA stood at 1.32%; net NPA was 0.17%.
- Provision coverage ratio remained above 86%.
- Current credit cost stood at 31 bps.
- FY27 credit-cost guidance remains 50–60 bps.
- Management expects credit costs near the lower end.
- No corporate slippages were reported during the quarter.
- Microfinance performance has improved.
- El Niño and ECL transition remain potential risks.
- Management continues monitoring geopolitical and weather-related risks.

Fee Income & Operating Efficiency
- Fee-to-average-assets ratio stood at 1.11%.
- Distribution, processing, trade and treasury supported fee income.
- Insurance contributes meaningfully to fee income.
- Proposed insurance guidelines could affect commission income.
- One-off security receipts sale contributed approximately ₹30–35 Cr.
- Management continues focusing on costs and credit discipline.
- Resident savings grew 5%; CASA improved 103 bps YoY.

Capital & Expansion Strategy
- Capital adequacy remained comfortably above 16.8%.
- Pending 75% warrant conversion worth approximately ₹6,200 Cr supports capital.
- Management sees no immediate need for fresh capital.
- Existing capital is expected to support growth for 12–18 months.
- Expansion interests include affordable housing, micro-LAP and cards.
- Securities, AMC, wealth and SME businesses remain potential opportunities.
- No active inorganic acquisition discussions are underway.
- Management favours smaller strategic acquisitions over large deals.
- Any acquisition must fit strategy and offer attractive valuation.

Key Takeaway
- Strong profitability, loan growth and improving margins support momentum.
- FCNR(B) funding and deposit costs remain key NIM monitorables.
- Asset quality remains healthy, though agricultural and ECL risks persist.
- Capital position supports near-term growth without immediate fundraising.
- Impact: Positive

PNB – MANAGEMENT INTERVIEW AFTER Q2FY27 RESULTS
#Q2FY27

Financial Performance
- Net profit increased 13% YoY to ₹5,532 Cr.
- Core operating profit grew 29% during the quarter.
- Fee-based income increased over 16–19% YoY across management commentary.
- RoA stood at 1.05%, meeting guidance of above 1%.
- Management targets RoA of approximately 1.10%, with 1.04–1.06% expected to remain sustainable.

Credit Growth & Business Outlook
- Global advances grew 14.7% YoY.
- Retail advances grew above 16%; agriculture above 18%.
- MSME growth reached approximately 20%, while corporate growth exceeded 10%.
- Management expects another 1–2% growth across key segments in Q3.
- More than ₹2.5 lakh Cr of corporate loans were sanctioned in H1.
- Full-year corporate loan sanctions could reach approximately ₹5 lakh Cr.
- Credit growth outlook ranges from 11–12% to 14–15% across management commentary.
- Deposit growth guidance ranges from 9–10% to 13–14%.
- Management sees room to increase the credit-deposit ratio from 75% to 77–80%.

NIM & Interest Rate Outlook
- Global NIM improved 8 bps QoQ to 2.58%.
- Domestic NIM increased 10 bps to 2.74%, versus 2.64% in Q1.
- Global NIM guidance remains 2.6–2.8%.
- Management expects approximately 7 bps NIM improvement from the 25 bps repo-rate hike.
- A further 25 bps rate change in Q4 could add around 4 bps.
- Total potential NIM improvement could reach approximately 10 bps by March 2027.
- Around 56% of assets are linked to EBLR and 8% to TBLR.
- Shedding low-yielding advances and ₹50,000 Cr of IBPC supported margin improvement.
- Deposit repricing will be considered at the month-end ALCO meeting.

Funding & Deposit Management
- PNB mobilised US$2.7 billion in FCNR deposits against a US$2.5 billion target.
- FCNR funds helped reduce high-cost bulk deposits and certificates of deposit.
- High-cost certificates of deposit reduced by approximately ₹22,000 Cr.
- CD balances were reportedly ₹23,000–28,000 Cr below March levels.
- Global cost of deposits stood at 4.96%, down 22 bps YoY and 3 bps QoQ.
- The bank has stayed out of the CD market for six months.
- Liquidity coverage ratio stood at 133%, supporting funding flexibility.

Asset Quality & Credit Costs
- Gross NPA stood at 2.55%; net NPA was 0.25%.
- Gross NPA target remains below 2.50%.
- SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 together represented 2.49% of loans.
- Management considers the SMA book controlled and below its 4% tolerance level.
- Fresh sequential slippages totalled ₹2,395 Cr.
- Two corporate accounts contributed approximately ₹300 Cr to slippages.
- Provision coverage ratio stood at 97.32%.
- Credit cost was 0.25%, with FY27 guidance of 0.25–0.30%.
- Potential pressure factors include El Niño, rate hikes and pending agricultural renewals.
- Management is monitoring borrowers from the SMA-0 stage onward.

ECL Provisioning
- Estimated ECL requirement stands at approximately ₹8,000 Cr.
- This is lower than the earlier estimate of ₹9,000–9,500 Cr.
- Floating provisions already available total ₹2,560 Cr.
- Additional standard-asset provisions of ₹1,150 Cr were made during Q2.
- Management estimates a remaining requirement of approximately ₹4,500 Cr.
- The estimated capital adequacy impact is around 50–52 bps.
- Management expects existing provisions to support the April 2027 transition.
- Management does not anticipate a material profitability or capital challenge.

Treasury & Other Income
- Treasury profit declined to approximately ₹700 Cr from ₹1,700 Cr.
- Hardening government bond yields caused mark-to-market losses.
- Management expects treasury income to improve if government bond yields soften.
- Tighter foreign-exchange hedging norms are not expected to materially affect treasury income.
- Written-off account recoveries declined to around ₹800 Cr from ₹900 Cr.
- Management expects written-off account recoveries above ₹2,500 Cr in FY27.
- Potential aviation account recovery of ₹700 Cr is expected in Q3–Q4FY27.

Key Takeaway
- Improving NIM, loan growth and fee income support operating performance.
- FCNR mobilisation is helping reduce high-cost funding.
- Asset quality remains controlled, with low credit costs.
- ECL provisioning and treasury volatility remain key monitorables.
- Impact: Positive, with provisioning and funding risks

LTM – MANAGEMENT INTERVIEW AFTER Q2FY27 RESULTS
#Q2FY27

Revenue & Business Performance
- Revenue grew 1.1% QoQ in reported currency.
- Constant-currency revenue growth stood at 5.1% YoY.
- Middle East impact was estimated at 60–70 bps.
- Excluding Saudi Arabia, sequential growth would have been nearly 1.8%.
- Three of four verticals delivered above 7% YoY growth.
- BFS recorded sequential growth in both Q1 and Q2.

FY27 Growth Outlook
- Management expects FY27 growth to match or exceed FY26.
- H2FY27 growth expected to be better than H1FY27.
- Macroeconomic conditions and customer demand remain broadly unchanged.
- Saudi Arabia business weakness remains a near-term growth headwind.

AI Business Momentum
- AI revenue grew 40% YoY.
- AI contributed approximately 13–13.5% of quarterly revenue.
- Customers are shifting from proofs of concept to enterprise deployments.
- Management expects AI momentum to continue.
- Focus areas include Enterprise AI, Business AI, Industrial AI, and Marketing & Creative AI.
- Newer AI offerings increasingly address customer business processes beyond IT.

Order Inflow & Deal Pipeline
- Q2 order inflow stood at US$1.26 billion.
- Q1 order inflow was US$1.7 billion.
- Year-ago order inflow stood at US$1.5 billion.
- Book-to-bill ratio remained around 1.
- Traditional vendor-consolidation deals typically run 3–5 years.
- New AI-led deals generally have shorter 6–8 month tenures.
- Management views this as a shift in deal structure, not weakening demand.
- Follow-on AI projects may emerge as existing engagements conclude.

Key Takeaway
- AI growth and broad-based vertical performance support the outlook.
- Management expects stronger growth in H2FY27.
- Saudi Arabia weakness and lower order inflows require monitoring.
- Shorter AI deal tenures may create recurring follow-on opportunities.
- Impact: Mixed to Positive

YES BANK – MOODY'S AFFIRMS RATINGS
Credit Rating Update

Key Rating Actions
- Long-term foreign currency issuer rating reaffirmed at Ba1.
- Long-term local and foreign currency deposit ratings maintained at Ba1.
- Baseline Credit Assessment (BCA) reaffirmed at ba2.
- Adjusted BCA maintained at ba2.
- Senior unsecured medium-term note programme affirmed at (P)Ba1.
- Outlook remains Stable.

Rating Rationale
- Moody's expects the bank to sustain its credit profile.
- Improving funding trends support the rating.
- Gross NPA declined to 1.2% as of September 2026.
- Net income to tangible assets improved to 0.8% in H1FY27.
- Government of India support expectations underpin deposit ratings.

Capital & Liquidity
- Supreme Court ruling on AT1 write-downs may weaken capital ratios.
- Management estimates pro-forma CET1 at 11.4% as of September 2026.
- Bank expects to replenish capital buffers through fresh equity.
- Liquidity coverage ratio stood at 131% in Q2FY27.
- Funding profile has improved but remains weaker than large peers.

Outlook & Key Risks
- Normalising provisioning costs may support profitability.
- Ratings could improve with stronger standalone credit quality or support.
- Significant funding or asset-quality deterioration could trigger downgrades.
- Capital weakening without a credible fundraising plan remains a risk.

Key Takeaway
- Stable ratings reflect improving asset quality and profitability.
- AT1-related capital pressure remains a key monitorable.
- Fresh equity raising will be important for capital buffers.
- Impact: Neutral to Positive

Curious when FII will come back to India

So gave Co-pilot a prompt
“Why FIIs wont return to India even as AI trade unwind globally”

Reverse Psychology

Here is the response

1. India is still expensive vs EM peers
o Even after corrections, India trades at a premium to most emerging markets.
o FIIs compare India with China, Korea, Taiwan, Brazil, not with India's own history.
o If China is at 10-12x PE and India at 20-25x PE, capital tends to chase cheaper markets. 
2. India lacks direct AI beneficiaries
o The AI trade created winners in US tech, Taiwan semiconductors and Korean memory-chip companies.
o India has very few large listed AI, semiconductor or hyperscaler plays that global thematic funds can buy. 
3. Dollar returns matter, not rupee returns
o FIIs think in USD.
o Even if Nifty is flat or slightly up, rupee depreciation can wipe out returns.
o Currency risk remains a major deterrent for foreign capital. 
4. US yields remain a strong competitor
o If US Treasuries offer attractive risk-free returns, FIIs need a much higher expected return from India.
o Many global allocators prefer earning 4-5% in dollar assets rather than taking EM risk. 
5. India's earnings growth has moderated
o India's premium valuation was justified when earnings were compounding rapidly.
o If earnings growth slows while valuations remain rich, FIIs question the risk-reward. 
6. Better opportunities elsewhere
o Korea, Taiwan and China offer exposure to AI, semiconductors and manufacturing at lower valuations.
o Global funds have finite capital; India is competing against these markets for allocation. 
7. India is no longer an under-owned market
o After years of strong inflows, most EM funds already have meaningful India exposure.
o Incremental flows require a new catalyst, not just the absence of AI enthusiasm.
8. Domestic flows reduce urgency
o SIPs, mutual funds and insurance money continue supporting Indian markets despite FII selling.
o Paradoxically, this resilience prevents large valuation corrections that would otherwise attract FIIs back.

Maruti Suzuki India should be rechristened as Suzuki India

Maruti's journey started as a Govt of India project. Maruti Udyog was the Indian promoter & Suzuki was brought in as the technology partner. Back then, this was very much an Indian company with Japanese know-how.

Over time, the Indian promoter gradually diluted its holding & eventually exited completely. Suzuki did the opposite, staying invested through every cycle & steadily increasing its stake.

What began as a JV slowly became Suzuki's most important global asset. The ownership story itself tells you who has deepened commitment over the decades.

For years, investors debated why Suzuki was setting up fresh manufacturing capacity outside Maruti Suzuki through its Gujarat subsidiary instead of housing it directly in the listed entity.

Then came the reversal. Suzuki transferred Suzuki Motor Gujarat into Maruti Suzuki at a valuation of roughly ₹12,000+ Cr. Rather than taking cash, it largely took equity.

The result? Suzuki's ownership in Maruti Suzuki moved up further without having to buy equivalent shares from the secondary market.

This wasn't just a restructuring exercise. It was Suzuki effectively converting manufacturing assets into a larger stake in India's largest PV company.

Even after that transaction, Suzuki did not stop. It has periodically picked up additional shares from the open market whenever opportunities emerged.

The message is clear. The Indian promoter exited long ago. The Japanese promoter keeps doubling down on India.

Look at the cars on the road today. The branding emphasis is on the giant "S" logo. 10-15years back, cars started selling with only “S” logo, 1st on premium nexa cars, then on all the models. You will hardly see Maruti branded cars on road now

For many younger buyers, the brand recall is shifting from "Maruti Suzuki" to simply "Suzuki". The transition is subtle but visible.

India is now the crown jewel of Suzuki Motor Corp. A substantial portion of Suzuki valuation come from Indian listed entity. Maruti $38bn mcap translate to $21bn (for 58% stake, $15bn if applied 30% Holdco disc).

Even beyond that, Maruti pays over $500m to Suzuki as royalty, that value must be over $5bn in the SoTP of Suzuki motors. Suzuki motors also have successful 2w biz in India, they are 6th largest 2w in India, clocking over 1lac units every month

In many ways, investors buying Suzuki Motor Corp are indirectly buying the India story. Cars sold by Suzuki in India is higher than overall car sold by Suzuki in other 100 countries combined

A rebranding to "Suzuki India" could also help shed the old "cheap small-car company" perception. As premium SUVs, hybrids & future EVs gain share, a stronger global MNC identity may command a different customer mindset.

Ownership, capital allocation, manufacturing integration, branding & growth strategy all point in one direction: this is increasingly Suzuki's India story.

Conclusion: Maruti only stays in Co. name hence should be renamed now

What regulators see that investors often ignore 👇

Every time a regulator acts, investors first ask: "How much EPS gets hit?" Regulators ask something else: "Is the market structure fair for the end consumer?" That's a very different lens. 
Thoughts on recent #PBFintech & older #IEX n more

Case in point: Recent change on insurance commissions. The proposed changes effectively aim to reduce distribution costs & curb excessive upfront payouts on some products. Investors see lower margins. Regulators see lower customer acquisition costs & better value for policyholders.

Truth is, hardly anyone argues that insurance has zero mis-selling. Higher upfront commissions have often created incentives to sell what pays the most, not what suits the customer best. If that problem exists, intervention shouldn't be surprising.

The irony is that many investors celebrate efficiency in every industry except their own portfolio holdings. When a regulator targets excess distribution costs, the reaction is often outrage instead of introspection.

Look at insurance expense ratios. Even as the industry scaled up, commission/expense pools as a % of premium remained elevated in several segments. The regulator's job is to ask: why isn't scale translating into lower customer costs?

Learning from MFs TER. Every TER cut was seen as fatal attack. Prediction was: growth will die, distributors will vanish, profit collapse. Instead industry adapted. Players became efficient, direct plans gained share, technology reduced costs, investor participation & AUM surged

Market coupling in power exch. Investors focus: which exchange lose market share. Regulators focus: consumers get better price discovery. Market coupling means bids/orders from all exch get pooled to discover a single price. One price improves efficiency & reduces fragmentation

Could one exchange lose moat? Maybe. But from system perspective, better price discovery, deeper liquidity & lower market distortion are hard to ignore.
Regulators rarely optimize for shareholder returns. They optimize for consumers, market efficiency & long-term public interest

Think about hospitals. If tomorrow there is stricter price regulation, hospital stocks may get hit. As investors we'd feel the pain. But can anyone honestly deny healthcare costs are becoming unaffordable for a large section of Indians?
One may argue India's healthcare is still cheaper than many countries. True. But the person comparing prices globally is not the same person struggling to pay a hospital bill locally.

Markets often assume regulators must protect industry profitability. Regulators believe industries shouldn't fleece poor customers. When public benefit & industry profits collide, the regulator's choice is usually obvious.

That's why stock market reaction is often the last variable in the regulator's decision. If a policy improves consumer outcomes, transparency, affordability or efficiency, temporary shareholder pain rarely changes the outcome.
